newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: LONE BODY IS GRIM VESTIGE OF GUATEMALA TRAGEDY.
newsitem.headline: LONE BODY IS GRIM VESTIGE OF GUATEMALA TRAGEDY.

text.p: "Male XX from the stadium, 30-40 years old" lay in front of the gate to the main morgue, his dead body swollen, blood lining his face, a lonely reminder of a tragedy that engulfed Guatemala a day earlier.

Within hours of a stampede of fans at Guatemala's overcrowded national soccer stadium that killed at least 80 people, Guatemalans, distraught with grief, lined up at the morgue late on Wednesday, searching for loved ones lost at the game.
Of the 78 corpses at the morgue, all but one had been accounted for by Thursday afternoon amid an agony of weeping by relatives, some who fainted with grief.
Surrounded by scores of curious onlookers, morgue official Olvidio Arana Salazar, an elderly man in a white cap, sought in vain to find a mourner for the last body in his care.

"Male XX has no documents, can anyone identify him? Come in two by two, no children," Arana shouted. But no one came, except curiosity-seekers pressed up against the gate, close enough to touch the bare-footed corpse in worn trousers.

Of those who died, most were poor Guatemalans, who spent as much as $7 for a ticket to the Guatemala-Costa Rica World Cup soccer qualifier. They were suffocated beneath a cascade of bodies after a sudden surge in the packed stadium.
National soccer officials admitted the stadium was overcrowded and blamed scalpers for selling fake tickets.
Amid the grief, relatives, many impoverished Indians, blamed top officials for not showing up at the morgue and said greed may have been behind the tragedy.
"This is a tragedy that should have been prevented. It was corruption that let this happen because of all the forged tickets," a grieving boy said.

Others said the authorities should pay for the costly burials. "The money they charged for the tickets should be passed on to the families of the dead," said Marina Hernandez, as she read a list of the dead.
Soccer officials said proceeds from the ticket sales were frozen in a bank account pending an investigation.
At the wreath stall next door to the morgue, locals did brisk business but took no pleasure from the windfall.
